Brazil swings right as Bolsonaro tops Lula in first round

Todayville

Published

22 hours ago

6 minute read

  MxM News

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:30
Instaread

Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro came out on top in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election Sunday, outperforming expectations and forcing left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva into an Oct. 25 runoff.

With roughly 99 percent of ballots counted, Bolsonaro held 47.2 percent of the vote to Lula’s 44.9 percent, a significant reversal from preelection polling that largely showed the incumbent holding a narrow lead.

The result gives Bolsonaro a major boost heading into the second round and adds Brazil to a growing list of Latin American countries where right-wing candidates aligned with President Trump have gained ground.

Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, ran especially strong across Brazil’s populous south and southeast.

In São Paulo, the country’s largest state, Bolsonaro led Lula roughly 52 percent to 38 percent. He also carried Minas Gerais, a state long viewed as a bellwether in Brazilian politics, by about 48 percent to 43 percent.

In Rio de Janeiro, another Bolsonaro stronghold, the senator posted an even wider margin, leading Lula 53 percent to 39 percent.

Lula remained dominant across much of Brazil’s northeast, piling up large margins in Bahia, Pernambuco and Ceará. But those victories were not enough to offset Bolsonaro’s strength elsewhere.

The outcome immediately raised fresh questions about Brazilian polling, which had generally placed Lula ahead going into election day.

The Bolsonaro movement has long accused major Brazilian polling firms of producing surveys that favor Lula and his left-wing Workers’ Party, complaints that are likely to intensify following Sunday’s result.

Similar polling misses surrounded Jair Bolsonaro’s campaigns in both 2018 and 2022, although Sunday’s disparity between expectations and the final first-round results was particularly striking.

Flávio Bolsonaro also benefited from a close relationship with President Trump, who made clear during the campaign that he wanted to see Lula defeated.

The Brazilian result follows a series of recent conservative gains across Latin America, including victories by right-leaning political movements in Chile, Argentina, Peru, Ecuador and Bolivia.

For Lula, the disappointing showing could reopen debate over whether the 80-year-old president should have sought another term at all.

Lula has already served three terms as president and is now pursuing a fourth. He returned to power in 2022 after his corruption convictions were annulled and defeated Jair Bolsonaro by an extremely narrow margin.

Lula had previously indicated that his current term would be his last, only to reverse course and seek reelection.

Despite the setback, Lula remains a formidable campaigner with a powerful political organization and deep support in parts of the country. The runoff remains competitive, and three weeks of campaigning could still reshape the race.

Bolsonaro, however, enters the second round with several potential advantages.

Four major third-party candidates — Augusto Cury, Renan Santos, Ronaldo Caiado and Romeu Zema — combined for nearly 8 percent of the first-round vote. Bolsonaro is expected to compete heavily for those voters, with Caiado and Zema viewed as particularly likely sources of support.

Any formal endorsements could prove decisive in a race that remains relatively close.

A Bolsonaro victory would also carry enormous consequences for his family and for Brazil’s political establishment.

Flávio Bolsonaro is widely expected to seek the release of his father and senior Brazilian military officials jailed over accusations that they participated in a plot to keep Jair Bolsonaro in power following the 2022 election.

The Bolsonaro family also posted victories elsewhere Sunday.

Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won election to the Senate, as did his son Carlos Bolsonaro, while another son, Renan Bolsonaro, won a seat in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies.

The family’s Liberal Party also performed strongly in congressional races.

The party is expected to control 29 seats in the Senate compared with nine for Lula’s Workers’ Party. In the lower chamber, the Liberal Party is projected to hold 121 seats, making it the largest bloc, while the left-wing Brazil Fe coalition is expected to finish with 78.

Political analyst Flavio Morgenstern argued that the election represented something larger than a contest between Lula and Bolsonaro.

“This election was not about Flavio Bolsonaro vs. Lula,” Morgenstern said. “It’s about all of freedom-loving Brazil against the Brazilian Supreme Court.”

The Bolsonaro movement has spent years battling Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court, whose actions against Jair Bolsonaro and his allies have become a central rallying point for the Brazilian right.

Sunday’s results leave Flávio Bolsonaro with momentum, a strengthened congressional movement and a clear path to consolidating much of the anti-Lula vote.

The War Behind The War: IRGC Mistake Confirms Trump’s Hit on the British Empire

Published on October 5, 2026

By

Todayville

 Susan Kokinda

Day after day, it’s becoming more obvious just who is fighting who in all the major conflicts around the world.  Last week, the IRGC released an open letter to American voters.  In it, Iran blames Trump, the CIA, Israel and Wall Street, basically asking US voters to support the Democrats during next month’s midterms.

In today’s video from Promethean Action, Susan Kokinda opens with the 25-page open letter Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps addressed to the American people weeks before the midterms. The State Department dismissed the letter as a desperate  attempt and the Daily Wire read it as a plea for Americans to vote Democrat.  Kokinda argues the letter tells a bigger story than anyone is reporting: it names the CIA, Israel and the military-industrial complex, but never once the British who have been very busy in Iran over the years.  It’s a very intentional ommission.

After President Trump’s “easy way or the hard way” remark on Iran, and his statement at the U.N. that the election won’t influence his Iran policy, the episode revisits the 1953 overthrow of Mohammad Mosaddegh, whom the letter calls an “Americanophile,” after he nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, today’s BP.

Susan cites National Security Archive documents showing the British Foreign Office approached the Truman administration in late 1952 to propose a coup in Iran. It then turns to a Foreign Affairs newsletter citing the 1956 Suez crisis as a parallel to the war with Iran, President Eisenhower’s refusal to back Britain and France at Suez, and Gamal Abdel Nasser’s 1955 Foreign Affairs article on how the British ran Egypt.

Kokinda closes this video with Richard Haass on Morning Joe, the morning after Trump’s U.N. speech, calling it “the end of 80 years of American foreign policy,” Chatham House director Bronwen Maddox on Europe having to defend itself against the U.S., and Mark Carney telling the New York Times he spent the past year preparing for the “extreme tail risk” of U.S. military action against Canada.

Various actions by the Trump Presidential Administration make sense when you see them as part of the battle between the American system and the Globalists.

The Willful Blindness of Premier David Eby to the alleged impact of corrupt foreign interference has resulted in a dysfunctional democracy in British Columbia

Published on October 5, 2026

By

Todayville

By Elbert King Paul, CPA, CA

“B.C. voters would like to know who was lobbying whom when BC Ferries awarded a $1.5 billion contract to CMI Weihai, which would support state-owned Chinese shipyards.”

First pride, then the crash – the bigger the ego, the harder the fall. Proverbs 16:18, The Message

“Nobody but David Eby wants this B.C. Election” – “It’s naked opportunism, without the dignity or even gesturing towards subtlety,” reports Kirk Lapointe in The Hub on September 22, 2026.

However, this election presents a critical opportunity for voters to examine the issues highlighted that same day in The Bureau’s report, “Public Safety documents flag intelligence, military base and supply chain risks in BC Ferries China deal.” That report brings necessary attention to Premier Eby’s handling of foreign interference and its impact on British Columbia’s political process.

Firstly, of major relevance is the 2022 Cullen Commission report focused on networks of transnational organized crime and money laundering, networks linked to foreign interference, including election meddling, according to The Bureau‘s reporting.

Gordon Hoekstra of The Vancouver Sun reported on December 9, 2024, that Premier Eby had delayed or sidelined two of the most significant structural changes requested by Commissioner Austin Cullen:

  1. An Independent Anti-Money Laundering Commissioner: Recommended to act as an independent legislative “czar” to provide strategic oversight, conduct research, and keep the public informed on B.C.’s anti-money laundering mandate.
  2. A Dedicated Provincial Intelligence and Investigation Unit: Recommended to bypass perceived federal enforcement gaps (such as shortfalls within FINTRAC and the RCMP) by introducing a specialized provincial policing unit focused strictly on illicit financial flows.

The conscious avoidance by Premier Eby of implementing the two major recommendations in the Cullen Report is a breach of his duty to the citizens of B.C. and enables foreign interference to undermine our liberal democracy, impacting government transparency and accountability and the rule of law.

Secondly, Premier Eby’s complete failure to protect British Columbians from foreign interference arose when BC Ferries awarded a contract to China’s Weihai Shipyards (CMI Weihai) to build four new Summit-class hybrid-electric vessels. This contract was backed by a $1 billion low-interest loan from the Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB). The deal has triggered intense political backlash, including concerns over lobbying, and has caused parliamentary committee investigations.

The federal government’s Public Safety Records Assessment of the controversial BC Ferries contract with a Chinese state-owned shipyard identified potential risks to Canadian supply chains. The assessment flagged the proximity of ferry routes to sensitive military and intelligence infrastructure — including a Signals Intelligence facility in Haida Gwaii and the country’s main naval base in Victoria.

Rob Shaw reported on August 12, 2025, in Business in Vancouver that Davie Shipyard, the oldest and highest-capacity shipyard in the country, located in Quebec, criticized BC Ferries for a flawed procurement process. The company said the contract was tilted from the start to award new ship construction contracts to the government of China. Davie Shipyard stated BC Ferries never gave Canadian builders a real chance at competing for the billion-dollar contract to build four new large ships.

A 2026 report by the Centre for Future Work estimated that the offshore build will result in roughly $1.5 billion in lost Canadian economic activity (GDP) and 10,000 missed job-years. This lost revenue is profoundly disquieting in light of the September 18, 2026, National Post reporting that in his tenure so far, Premier David Eby has presided over the fastest rate of debt accumulation in the province’s history. Total B.C. debt stood at $89.4 billion on Eby’s first day in office and is now projected to reach $180 billion by 2027.

Critics of BC Ferries’ $1.5 billion contract with CMI Weihai question the involvement of Dominic Barton, former McKinsey & Company global managing director and former Canadian Ambassador to China. Mr. Barton helped develop the CIB, resulting in ongoing debates in parliamentary committees over Barton’s corporate influence networks and McKinsey’s advisory ties to Chinese state-owned enterprises. Prime Minister Mark Carney recently appointed Barton to chair the board of Invest in Canada, which connects multinational corporations to opportunities to grow, expand and succeed in Canada.

Section 2(1)(f) of the B.C. Lobbyists Transparency Act excludes communications between the Government of British Columbia and representatives of international governments such as China.

B.C. voters would like to know who was lobbying whom when BC Ferries awarded a $1.5 billion contract to CMI Weihai, which would support state-owned Chinese shipyards tied to Beijing’s industrial-military framework. Premier Eby’s profound lack of government transparency and accountability over lobbying by China, or its proxies, of BC Ferries raises legitimate questions.

The benefits that authentic liberal democracies confer on their citizens are substantial. These include individual rights, separation of powers, economic opportunity and equality, government transparency and accountability, rule of law and self-critique.

Premier Eby’s wilful blindness to the alleged impact of corrupt foreign interference as detailed in the Cullen Report and the secretive process of awarding a $1.5 billion contract to CMI Weihai has resulted in a dysfunctional democracy in B.C.

We are challenged and encouraged by the lyrics of our National Anthem: “O Canada, we stand on guard for thee. God keep our land glorious and free!”

Elbert King Paul is a Chartered Accountant and CPA, and a former director and chair of the Audit Committee of the Federal Liberal Agency of Canada (FLAC). He served during the tenures of seven Liberal Party of Canada leaders, including four prime ministers. Paul is also a former partner at a major national accounting firm.
